extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners, patent prosecutors, and patent practitioners (those examining or preparing U.S. patent applications)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and procedural standards for determining whether a patent application specification satisfies the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 112, ¶1). Focuses on how examiners should evaluate original, amended, and newly added claims for adequate support and absence of new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description Requirement — Purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: The specification shall contain a written description of the invention; this requirement is separate and distinct from enablement and serves to demonstrate that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention and to put the public in possession of what is claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains policy objectives: convey that applicant invented the claimed subject matter, disclose technology upon which patent is based, and promote public knowledge. Cites cases (e.g., Capon v. Eshhar, Regents v. Eli Lilly) and stresses that the requirement implements the disclosure/possession principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification Must Show Possession to One Skilled in the Art
rubrics_metrics.description: To satisfy the written description requirement, the specification must describe the claimed invention in sufficient detail that one skilled in the art can reasonably conclude the inventor had possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Possession may be shown by words, structures, figures, diagrams, and formulas; examples include reduction to practice, drawings or structural chemical formulas, or identifying distinguishing characteristics. Written description is a fact-based inquiry that varies with the nature of the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possession Requires Description of All Claim Limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant shows possession of the claimed invention by describing the claimed invention with all of its limitations using descriptive means (words, structures, figures, diagrams, formulas) that fully set forth the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner should ensure the claimed invention as a whole is described; mere functional statements without structure or identifying characteristics may be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description Is Distinct From Enablement
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with the written description requirement is a separate inquiry from enablement; proof of enablement does not necessarily prove written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites case law (e.g., Vas-Cath, In re Curtis) illustrating that enablement (how to make/use) and written description (possession) are different analyses and both must be considered in examination when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original Claims — Strong Presumption of Adequate Written Description
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a strong presumption that an adequate written description of the claimed invention is present when the application is filed; the PTO has the initial burden of presenting reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize support for the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections of original claims for lack of written description should be rare. Nonetheless, even original claims can fail if an essential or critical feature of the claim is not described with sufficient particularity in the specification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim-As-A-Whole Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: For each claim, determine what the claim as a whole covers (including preamble and transitional phrase) and analyze support for the claim as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim construction is essential; apply the broadest reasonable interpretation consistent with the specification. Consider preamble language, transitional phrases (comprising, consisting essentially of, consisting of) and weight given to the preamble when evaluating written description support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate Sufficiency of Structures, Acts, or Functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners should evaluate whether sufficient structures, acts, or functions are recited to make clear the scope and meaning of the claim, including the weight to be given the preamble.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absence of detail for well-established terms should not automatically justify a written description rejection. Determine whether the claim recites enough to show possession to one skilled in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transition Phrase Effects on Scope and Support
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional phrases affect claim scope: 'comprising' is open-ended; 'consisting essentially of' occupies a middle ground; 'consisting of' is closed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For prior art searches and scope determination, if the specification does not define what is 'basic and novel' the middle ground phrase may be construed as open-ended. Applicant bears burden to show exclusion of additional elements where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original Claims Can Constitute Their Own Description
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfactory description may be in the claims or any other portion of the originally filed specification; original claims can serve as part of the disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical cases (In re Koller, In re Gardner) support that claims may provide descriptive content; however, quality and specificity of that description still matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genus/Species Support Requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A generic disclosure of a genus or a 'laundry list' of possible moieties does not necessarily provide written description support for every species within that genus unless the disclosure reasonably leads skilled artisans to those species.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases (e.g., Fujikawa, In re Ruschig) illustrate that mere recitation of many possibilities without guidance to particular species can fail written description for particular claimed species or ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional Descriptions of Biomolecules Usually Insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: A biomolecule sequence described only by a functional characteristic, without any known or disclosed correlation between that function and the structure, normally is not sufficient identifying characteristic for written description purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Functional claiming of sequences or products without structural identifying information will generally fail unless there is a known structure-function correlation or other identifying disclosure; compare software functional descriptions where function may be sufficient if coding is routine in the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: New or Amended Claims Must Be Supported by Original Disclosure (No New Matter)
rubrics_metrics.description: New or amended claims which introduce elements or limitations not supported by the as-filed disclosure violate the written description requirement; the prohibition on new matter prevents adding beyond the originally filed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support may be express, implicit, or inherent. Applicant may amend the specification to include original-claim material. See detailed MPEP cross-references (§2163.06-07).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correcting Obvious Errors May Be Permissible
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment to correct an obvious error does not constitute new matter where one skilled in the art would recognize both the error and the appropriate correction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: correction of sequencing errors may be permissible where resequencing would reveal a minor error; reliance on post-filing deposits for such corrections is limited and subject to CFR provisions and applicant statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post‑Filing Deposits Generally Cannot Support Additions
rubrics_metrics.description: Deposits made after the application filing date cannot be relied upon to support additions to or correction of information in the application as filed, except under narrow regulatory conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposits may support corrections only if applicant submits required statements (e.g., 37 CFR 1.804) and the deposited material corresponds to material specifically defined in the application as filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Omission of Limitation May Broaden Claims and Cause Lack of Possession
rubrics_metrics.description: Omission of a limitation that the specification treated as essential or critical can render a claim broader than the disclosed invention and lead to lack of adequate written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites examples (e.g., Gentry Gallery, PIN/NIP) where claims broadened by removing an essential element were invalid for lacking written description support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency — Implicit Disclosure of Function, Theory, or Advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: A device disclosed as inherently performing a function or having a property, operating according to a theory, or having an advantage, necessarily discloses that function/theory/advantage even if not explicit; such inherency may support later amendments without new matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To establish inherency, extrinsic evidence must show the missing matter is necessarily present and would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill; inherency cannot be premised on mere possibilities or probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incorporation by Reference Treated as Part of Application
rubrics_metrics.description: Material properly incorporated by reference is considered part of the application as filed and may be used to support claimed subject matter as if the text were repeated in the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refer to 37 CFR 1.57(a) and MPEP §608.01(p) for rules on incorporation by reference. Replacing incorporated material with the actual text is not new matter. Incorporation affects written description and 112(f) analyses per MPEP cross-references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written Description Issues Arise in Multiple Contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Adequacy of written description can arise for original claims, new/amended claims, claims seeking entitlement to earlier priority dates, and claims corresponding to counts in interference proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should be aware of varying fact patterns (e.g., priority claims under 35 U.S.C. 119/120/365(c), interference practice) and apply the written description inquiry case-by-case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden on Examiner and Applicant Regarding Support for Amendments
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners have the initial burden, after reading the application, to present evidence or reasons why persons skilled in the art would not recognize that the disclosure provides support for the claims; applicants should specifically point out support for amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant points out support and the examiner disagrees, the examiner must present evidence or reasoning why the disclosure does not reasonably convey possession. See MPEP §714.02, §2163.04.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adequacy Depends on Nature of the Invention and Predictability of the Art
rubrics_metrics.description: The level of written description required necessarily varies depending on the nature of the invention and the amount of knowledge imparted to those skilled in the art; predictability of the art is a relevant factor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In unpredictable arts (e.g., certain biotechnology), more detailed disclosure may be required for possession; in predictable arts, less detail may suffice. Consider whether persons skilled in the art could immediately envisage the product from a disclosed process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description Must Be Sufficient to Permit Verification for Deposited Biological Materials
rubrics_metrics.description: When a deposit of biological material is referenced, the written description must be sufficient to permit verification that the deposited material is as disclosed; deposit is not a substitute for a complete written description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deposited material must be described as completely as possible because patentability examination proceeds on the written description. Regulatory deposit rules (37 CFR 1.801 et seq.) and the Deposit of Biological Materials rule (54 Fed. Reg. 34,864) apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims That Omit Matter Described as Essential May Also Trigger Enablement/Definiteness Issues
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that omits matter disclosed to be essential in the specification may be subject to rejection under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (written description), 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (definiteness), or as not enabling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the specification makes clear a feature is essential or its location is the 'only possible' location, removing that feature may broaden the claim improperly; consider related MPEP sections (e.g., §2172, §2173).

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination Is Fact‑Intensive and Case‑By‑Case
rubrics_metrics.description: Compliance with the written description requirement is essentially a fact-based inquiry that necessarily varies depending on the nature of the invention claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner must weigh the specification disclosure, claim language, level of skill in the art, predictability, and relevant precedent to reach a written description determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient Detail for Software Best Mode vs Sequence Claims
rubrics_metrics.description: For software, disclosure of functions may suffice for best mode/description because writing code is often within the skill of the art; for nucleotide/amino acid sequences, mere function may not identify the claimed sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite Fonar v. GE (software functions acceptable in many cases) contrasted with sequence cases (In re Bell, In re Deuel) where structural identification is required. Evaluate according to skill level in art and predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: When Assessing Whether a Specification Provides Adequate Written Description, Consider Whether It Provides Identifying/Distinguishing Characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification may show possession by describing distinguishing identifying characteristics sufficient to show that the applicant was in possession of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include structural formulas, drawings, or specific descriptions rather than generic functional descriptions; one must define compounds or materials by characteristics that sufficiently distinguish them.
